promptText: Once an attacker achieves XSS execution on your origin, what makes it considered so severe?
options: Their injected script runs with the same access as your own legitimate code — it can read the DOM, steal tokens/cookies, and make authenticated requests as the logged-in user
It can only deface the page's visual appearance without accessing any application data
It is limited strictly to reading public HTML content already visible to any anonymous visitor
XSS payloads cannot make network requests, only display a JavaScript alert dialog
explanation: XSS means arbitrary JS execution on your origin, which is equivalent to full account takeover potential because the attacker's script inherits the victim's cookies, tokens, and ability to act as them.

promptText: Why does rendering {userInput} as a JSX child protect against XSS by default?
options: React HTML-encodes text children before inserting them, so a value like <script> is rendered as visible literal text rather than parsed as markup
React blocks any request whose body contains the literal word 'script'
React runs all rendered text through an antivirus scanner before rendering
JSX strips out any character in a string that is not alphanumeric
explanation: React auto-escapes text children so that special characters like < and > are HTML-encoded, meaning injected markup is displayed as text rather than parsed and executed.

promptText: Why is React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML named the way it is?
options: It sets the DOM node's innerHTML directly with no escaping at all, so any HTML or JavaScript in the string is parsed and can execute — the name is a deliberate warning
The API is deprecated and scheduled for complete removal in a future React version
It only functions correctly when passed HTML from trusted, first-party npm packages
It automatically pipes its input through DOMPurify internally before rendering
explanation: dangerouslySetInnerHTML is React's deliberate escape hatch that bypasses auto-escaping entirely, shifting full responsibility for safety onto the developer — hence the warning built into its name.

promptText: Why doesn't a strict CORS policy protect an API endpoint from being called by non-browser tools like curl or Postman?
options: CORS is enforced by the browser only — it governs whether JS in a browser can read a cross-origin response, and non-browser clients ignore it entirely, so the request itself often still reaches and executes on the server
curl and Postman requests are explicitly allow-listed by every server's default CORS configuration
CORS blocks all requests at the network layer before they can ever reach any server
CORS restrictions only apply to requests originating from localhost
explanation: CORS is purely a browser-enforced mechanism controlling whether JS can read a response; it never stops the request from being sent or executed, and any non-browser client bypasses it entirely — so authorization must live on the backend.

promptText: Why is embedding a real secret key in a Vite or CRA client-prefixed environment variable (e.g. VITE_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY) unsafe?
options: Build tools string-replace client-prefixed env vars directly into the shipped JS bundle as plaintext, making them readable by anyone who opens DevTools
Environment variables are automatically encrypted at build time and decrypted only by requests from the correct origin
The VITE_ and REACT_APP_ prefixes restrict the variable's visibility to the app's own domain only
Secrets stored in environment variables are visible only to the developer who originally defined them
explanation: Anything shipped to the browser is public by definition — client-prefixed env vars are baked into the bundle as plaintext at build time, so any real secret placed there is exposed to every visitor.

promptText: What is the core mechanic behind a clickjacking attack?
options: The attacker frames your page invisibly or disguised and positions bait UI so the user's click actually lands on a hidden, authenticated action inside your framed page
The attacker directly steals and replays the victim's mouse cursor coordinates over the network
The attacker modifies your site's own source code on the server without authorization
Clickjacking requires the victim to first manually disable JavaScript in their browser settings
explanation: Clickjacking (UI redressing) overlays your authenticated page in a transparent iframe under decoy bait UI, so a click the user thinks lands on something innocent actually executes an action inside your framed, logged-in session.

promptText: What makes DOM-based XSS uniquely dangerous compared to stored or reflected XSS?
options: The malicious payload can flow entirely through client-side sources (like location.hash) into a sink like innerHTML without ever being sent to the server, making it invisible to server logs and WAFs
DOM-based XSS is the only variant capable of stealing cookies from the victim's browser
DOM-based XSS only affects users running Internet Explorer and has no impact on modern browsers
DOM-based XSS requires the victim to manually paste attacker-supplied code into the browser console
explanation: Because the server is never involved, a DOM-based payload living only in the URL fragment is invisible to server-side defenses like WAFs and log-based filtering — it must be caught by client-side validation/escaping instead.

promptText: Why is a hand-rolled regex "sanitizer" that strips <script> tags considered unsafe compared to a library like DOMPurify?
options: Block-lists always miss adversarial cases (SVG payloads, obscure event handlers, mutation XSS), while DOMPurify uses a continuously-updated allow-list model where only known-safe tags/attributes survive
Regex-based sanitization executes more slowly than DOMPurify but is otherwise equally safe
DOMPurify doesn't actually remove any tags — it only flags suspicious markup for later manual review
Regex sanitizers fail to compile under strict TypeScript mode and throw a build-time error
explanation: Block-lists are brittle because attackers keep finding new vectors a fixed regex never anticipated; DOMPurify's allow-list approach and ongoing maintenance against new browser parsing quirks is what makes it durable.

promptText: What is the generally recommended token storage pattern for a SPA that balances XSS and CSRF exposure?
options: A short-lived access token kept in memory (a JS variable or React state) plus a long-lived, rotatable refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie
Always store both the access token and the refresh token in localStorage for implementation simplicity
Store the access token in a non-httpOnly cookie with SameSite=None for maximum cross-site compatibility
Disable cookies entirely and pass the access token as a URL query parameter on every request
explanation: This pattern minimizes blast radius: the in-memory access token is short-lived and never persisted to disk, while the httpOnly refresh cookie is invisible to JS and can be rotated and revoked server-side.

promptText: A cookie is set with SameSite=Lax. What happens when a user clicks a link on an external site that top-level-navigates to your app?
options: The cookie IS sent, because Lax allows cross-site top-level GET navigations while still blocking cross-site subrequests and POSTs
The cookie is never sent for any cross-site interaction whatsoever under SameSite=Lax
SameSite=Lax behaves identically to SameSite=Strict in every scenario, with no practical difference
The cookie is sent only if the destination page happens to also be served over HTTPS, regardless of SameSite
explanation: SameSite=Lax, the modern browser default, permits the cookie on cross-site top-level navigations (like following a link) while still blocking it on cross-site subrequests and POSTs, balancing usability with CSRF protection.

promptText: Why do modern strict Content Security Policies favor a nonce-based script-src over simply allow-listing trusted origins?
options: Origin allow-lists can be bypassed via compromised or open resources hosted on a trusted CDN, whereas a fresh per-response nonce means injected scripts (which lack it) are blocked even if attacker content lands on an allow-listed origin
Nonce-based policies are a legal requirement under GDPR for any site serving European users
Allow-listing origins is deprecated syntax that no modern browser supports at all
Nonce-based policies eliminate the need to serve the site over HTTPS
explanation: A host allow-list is leaky because trusted CDNs can host attacker-controlled files; a per-response nonce ties script execution to the server, which is exactly why nonce + strict-dynamic is recommended over broad origin allow-lists.

promptText: A server "fixes" a CORS error by reflecting whatever Origin header the request sends back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What vulnerability does this create?
options: Any malicious website can now make credentialed (cookie-attached) cross-origin requests to the API and read the response, effectively opening the API's authenticated data to every origin
It has no meaningful security impact, since Access-Control-Allow-Credentials only affects response compression settings
It only permits same-origin requests through, making this configuration strictly safer than a static allow-list
Reflecting the Origin header automatically strips all cookies from the request as a built-in browser safety measure
explanation: Reflecting any Origin plus enabling credentials is equivalent to allowing all origins to make authenticated requests and read private data — a real, common misconfiguration that defeats the purpose of restricting CORS at all.

promptText: A team has a solid CSRF token defense (the synchronizer token pattern) but is also vulnerable to a stored XSS on the same origin. Why does the CSRF protection no longer meaningfully help?
options: An attacker with XSS runs code in your origin's own context, so they can read the CSRF token directly from the DOM/cookie and include it in their own forged same-origin requests, bypassing the token check entirely
CSRF tokens are always stored in a browser location that XSS-injected scripts structurally cannot access under any circumstance
XSS and CSRF vulnerabilities are mutually exclusive and cannot coexist on the same application
CSRF tokens automatically and instantly rotate the moment any XSS payload is detected by the browser
explanation: CSRF defenses assume you're already free of XSS — if an attacker's script runs in your origin's context, same-origin requests (including reading the CSRF token) sail through just like your own legitimate app code.

promptText: Why was the OAuth2 implicit flow deprecated in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE for single-page apps?
options: Implicit flow returned tokens directly in the URL fragment, exposing them to browser history, referrer leaks, and logs with no protection against interception, whereas PKCE binds a one-time authorization code to the client that started the flow so a stolen code alone can't be redeemed
Implicit flow was removed specifically because it required a server-side client secret that browser-based SPAs cannot protect
PKCE is simply a faster reimplementation of the exact same implicit-flow mechanism with no meaningful security difference
Implicit flow was deprecated solely because it lacks support for refresh tokens
explanation: Implicit flow's token-in-URL-fragment design leaked tokens into history/logs/referrers with no interception protection; PKCE's code_verifier/code_challenge pairing ensures only the client that started the flow can redeem the authorization code.

promptText: Even after moving an auth token from localStorage to an httpOnly cookie, a pen-tester with a working XSS exploit can still perform authenticated actions as the victim. Why doesn't httpOnly fully neutralize the XSS risk?
options: httpOnly only prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie's value directly — it does not stop injected script from causing the browser to send authenticated same-origin requests, since the cookie is still attached automatically
httpOnly cookies are transmitted in plaintext even over HTTPS, which is the actual gap the pen-tester exploited
httpOnly is only enforced by Chrome and is silently ignored by every other browser engine
httpOnly protects exclusively against CSRF, and has never been intended to offer any protection related to XSS at all
explanation: httpOnly reduces blast radius (the token itself can't be exfiltrated) but doesn't stop XSS from acting as the user, because the browser still attaches the cookie to same-origin requests the injected script makes — preventing XSS remains the primary control.
